newsitem.title: ITALY: Magistrates investigate up to 50 in railway probe.
newsitem.headline: Magistrates investigate up to 50 in railway probe.

text.p: Magistrates said on Wednesday they were investigating up to 50 people in a snowballing graft probe sparked by the arrest of the head of Italy's state railway company, Lorenzo Necci.
Alberto Cardino, one of magistrates in the northwestern town of La Spezia, told reporters the number of names on the official list of investigation had risen to between 40 and 50.
Chief prosecutor Antonio Conte earlier denied comments by Cardino that politicians had also been caught up in the affair.

Those remarks, in response to questions, triggered unease in the government and on the financial markets in a flashback to the "Tangentopoli" (Bribesville) scandals of the early 1990s which toppled Italy's corrupt political old guard.

"In relation to some newspaper reports and the alarm that these have caused, I feel it is my duty to state that no politician is on the list of those being investigated by this office," Conte said in a statement.
"There are merely certain matters that we are evaluating. In any case, I exclude that, at least at this stage, members of the government are involved in the affair," he said.
Italy's latest corruption probe broke on Monday with news of the arrest of Necci, managing director of state railway Ferrovie dello Stato.

Necci, who is one of Italy's most prominent public sector executives and had been overseeing a planned multi-billion dollar high-speed rail project, was questioned by magistrates for about an hour at La Spezia jail on Wednesday.
His lawyers said he had provided "clarifications" to magistrates and that they would ask for him to be freed.
Judicial sources said tax police had searched Rome offices of three magistrates in connection with the investigation.
Cardino said three boxes of documents relating to the probe were being sent from Rome to La Spezia and that arrest warrants in the case ran to some 200 pages.
Necci was arrested at his country home near Rome on Sunday on suspicion of involvement in a host of crimes including fraud, embezzlement, false accounting, corruption and abuse of office.
At least five more people were arrested on Tuesday, including the head of an arms company and two magistrates.
Industry Minister Pier Luigi Bersani said the railway was "pretty likely" to undergo a change of management following Necci's arrest.
Investigators have not given specific details of the case. Media reports have said judicial sources indicate that the probe focuses on suspected bribes for lucrative rail contracts.
Cardino's tanatalising comments on Tuesday that some unnamed politicians could also be involved led to banner headlines speculating about a new political graft scandal.
Prime Minister Romano Prodi acknowledged on Tuesday that the arrest was "worrying for the image" of Italy, but insisted that his centre-left government, elected in April, was not touched.
Posts Minister Antonio Maccanico said on Wednesday that his friendship with Necci had fired unwarranted speculation that he might be involved. Criticising Cardino's comments, he said:
"You should either name names or keep quiet."

Necci's arrest was not the first time scandal has touched the railroad. In 1988, the whole board resigned in the so-called "Golden Sheets Affair" which revealed that FS paid $110 million simply for linen and paper sheets for its sleeper service.
